exchanges.question: With investors acutely focused on incretin pricing rather than volume, how do Lilly's margins hold up under a wide range of price scenarios, and how do the manufacturing investments already made strengthen the competitive moat?
exchanges.answer: Five or six quarters into the post-shortage world Lilly can pursue volume aggressively, and obesity behaves differently from other pharma categories: because so much is out of pocket (75% of ex-U.S. Mounjaro business and a meaningful U.S. portion), volume expands, perhaps non-linearly, when price falls, though there is a floor; pretty much every price reduction has produced a large volume expansion. The primary Q1 price effect was negotiated government outcomes, the MFN package with the Trump administration and China diabetes access at a meaningful price reduction where volume far outstripped the concession. Unit economics are driven by fixed costs that are sunk or unmovable, so Lilly has latitude at the margin; the X factor for long-term operating margin is investment in future medicines, with a record load of phase III programs and a very full phase I and II pipeline.

exchanges.question: What are the learnings from the better-than-expected international Mounjaro launch for the ramp and long-term opportunity, and should any impact be expected from generic semaglutide entering select markets?
exchanges.answer: Mounjaro is fully launched in more than 55 countries with very strong uptake and rapid share gains; Brazil and Korea, launched in H2 2025, already have an estimated 60% market share, and China has type 2 diabetes NRDL reimbursement. Only a few weeks of India data exist but generic semaglutide appears to be stimulating overall obesity market growth including Mounjaro, whose prescriptions are about 10% higher in recent weeks than before generics entered. With OUS share above 53% on average and many markets at U.S.-like Zepbound share, incremental share gains get harder, so growth will come from patient activation and penetration; expect very strong continued year-on-year growth and some sequential growth, with European holiday seasonality in the second half.

exchanges.question: How is the obesity market starting to segment, and where does it open up as retatrutide, Foundayo and then eloralintide reach the market?
exchanges.answer: With perhaps billions of people living with overweight or obesity, many will want medicines tailored to their needs; Lilly is in early innings and is now bringing in a third segment (orals) after GLP-1 single agonists and dual agonists. Retatrutide obviously plays to people seeking greater weight loss but Lilly sees opportunities for it across the spectrum of obesity; eloralintide could serve patients wanting a non-GLP-1 mechanism for tolerability reasons or be added on top of existing incretins for incremental weight loss. Lilly is also investing in less frequent dosing, additional metabolic benefits and ultra-long-acting genetic medicine approaches, believes it leads in most if not all of those spaces, and because many are tied to common manufacturing platforms it can support whichever proves most favorable; how share shakes out is hard to prognosticate.

exchanges.question: What is the strategy to activate Medicare patients, will the pull-through show up in Q4 or more in 2027, and how should persistence be thought about in this population given the attractive price point?
exchanges.responderTitle: President of Lilly USA and Global Customer Capabilities
exchanges.answer: Part D access for obesity medicines starts in July and there are millions of Part D beneficiaries already living with obesity; the Bridge program runs from July all through 2027, so it is a long trajectory. Education of physicians, pharmacies and consumers will take time, so expect a gradual path in 2026 as it starts and continued growth in 2027. The $50 a month copay is an important affordability element; Zepbound and Mounjaro already show great persistency relative to other chronic conditions and the copay and health benefits will only add to that.

exchanges.question: Strategically, what does Lilly need to see from its I&I, neuroscience or oncology franchises to match the scale of the obesity and metabolic business, and is business development the answer?
exchanges.answer: Those businesses are growing extremely fast; even without obesity and metabolic, Lilly would be the fastest or surely one of the fastest-growing pharmaceutical companies. Each of the three areas has very significant unmet need to scale into as medicines succeed, and Lilly likes what it has and its direction. Some of the scaling will come via business development, for example Centessa opens sleep-wake medicines and Orna opens immune reset.

exchanges.question: With a few weeks of launch data and roughly 15,000 patients started, how confident is Lilly in the framing that Foundayo's initial trajectory sits below oral Wegovy's and then accelerates in the back half; and what Foundayo contribution is factored into the revised guidance?
exchanges.responderTitle: President of Lilly USA and Global Customer Capabilities
exchanges.answer: It is early days but the trajectory is encouraging: active salesforce promotion began just over a week ago and broad channel availability two weeks ago; the three growth catalysts are HCP familiarity, access and consumer awareness. There are over 8,000 Foundayo prescribers, a third of whom had never written an oral GLP-1, with positive sentiment on efficacy and the no-hassle daily oral; commercial access at two large PBMs arrives by mid-May and Medicare at the beginning of July; just over 20,000 patients have been treated to date, 80% of them new to class; full-scale DTC and TV launch comes in Q3 once prescribers know the profile. Lucas: the guide increase reflects strength across the portfolio; the Foundayo plan was set at the start of the year and with three weeks of data it is tracking to expectations, with high confidence in the trajectory.

exchanges.question: With the Bridge program extended into 2027, what comes next for the Part D arrangement, and is Lilly working with stakeholders on a revision to secure longer-term Medicare access?
exchanges.answer: When Lilly signed with the administration everyone knew Bridge would be needed for a mid-year launch, with a commitment to 2027 as a contingency if Part D plans did not opt in at a certain rate; they did not, unsurprisingly given their margins and other Part D disruptions, so the government is extending Bridge as it said it would. Access at $50 a month is a compelling proposition that will drive persistency, and in an 18-month window population-level health improvements should start to appear, which sets up the 2028 discussion. He expects the government to lean hard into Part D plan participation in 2028 and normalizing obesity care as standard preventative treatment for seniors, with the evidence possibly in hand as 2027 ends; more news on 2028 plans is likely as Lilly exits 2026.

exchanges.question: With commercial coverage relatively stable year over year, what are the steps to convince employers to buy into the Employer Connect program and how do its mechanics work?
exchanges.responderTitle: President of Lilly USA and Global Customer Capabilities
exchanges.answer: Commercial access has been steady at around 50%. Employer Connect works with third parties to go to employers on the value of covering obesity care, differentiated by a transparent price known to all employers and flexibility in designing the employer-employee contribution. The 2026 selling cycle has already passed, so despite positive employer feedback the impact will be gradual in the back half of 2026 with incremental opt-ins most likely for 2027; growing real-world evidence on employee health and productivity should reinforce coverage decisions.

exchanges.question: As the DTC channel evolves, how will Lilly leverage its scale across the incretin portfolio there, and what on the commercial side will help drive additional coverage?
exchanges.answer: Consumers taking charge of their health through digital platforms is here to stay and a big part of the business, so Lilly will keep investing; expect continuous improvement in the U.S. consumer experience and national expansion of current offerings, and the platform could be useful for more preventative medicines, within regulation and law. Ilya: around 55% of Zepbound new patient starts come through self-pay, mostly via LillyDirect or telehealth, and about 45% of early Foundayo volume is coming through LillyDirect. Patrik: with very high OUS share already, patient activation will drive most growth; markets respond to activation efforts, though with a slower ramp, given low incretin penetration outside the U.S.

exchanges.question: Zepbound's Q1 U.S. figures (about 7 million TRx and $4.1 billion of sales) imply roughly $580 per prescription, or about $550 adjusting for one-timers, versus cash prices around $450; what explains the delta, or is IMS not capturing online channels?
exchanges.answer: The math is pretty spot on, even after normalizing for period-to-period adjustments. Carving out the MFN agreement from November, net prices have been relatively stable quarter on quarter, reflecting price discipline while volume grows significantly; LillyDirect prices, adjusted down starting in December, have also been very stable, and the remainder by difference is the commercial business that gets to the $550 net. Dave added that a reasonable amount of medical exception and OSA usage moves across channels at close to an undiscounted price, which is probably the missing piece of the math.

exchanges.question: How does the Foundayo launch compare with a traditional primary care launch, what is being accelerated or held back and why, given the extreme amount of inventory prepared for launch?
exchanges.responderTitle: President of Lilly USA and Global Customer Capabilities
exchanges.answer: The same three elements apply as in every primary care launch (prescriber base, access, consumer awareness), but access is coming unusually early with two of three PBMs activating in the next couple of weeks and Part D in July rather than the usual lag. DTC was activated from day one through digital, social media and out-of-home, and consumer sentiment on efficacy and no food or water restrictions is resonating; full DTC is being held until physicians understand Foundayo, though still earlier than normal; overall an accelerated path versus Trulicity, Mounjaro, Zepbound and Jardiance launches. Dave: the three major U.S. obesity products are all line extensions whereas Foundayo is a new molecule and brand starting from a lower awareness baseline that Lilly is hugely confident it can build; the inventory speaks to the international rollout, with 40 countries under review and launches in scaled markets expected as Lilly exits this year into next at one of the most accelerated cadences in industry history.

exchanges.question: What is Lilly's vision for regular U.S. employer insurance coverage of obesity drugs in coming years, versus coverage shifting toward greater participant cost-sharing through LillyDirect?
exchanges.answer: As a policy matter obesity and overweight medications should be broadly covered, and the July 1 Medicare start is a big step that often spills over into commercial by setting a standard. The category will ultimately look like other chronic markets such as diabetes and hypertension, but it will not be a straight line: 70% of adults have overweight or obesity, so it is the last benefit in and the easiest to say no to. Employer Direct creates alternative pathways to yes; Lilly (and likely Novo Nordisk) will keep publishing data showing these drugs are probably cost-effective at current prices, which have been trending down, and new indications in comorbid populations are a good unlock; expect incremental progress quarter on quarter with updates through guidance.
